messages.content:
Rate the following clinical vignette:

The Weight of Still Water

Omar is a forty-year-old software engineer who came to this country from Iran in his late twenties, building a quiet, ordered life that suited him - a wife he adores, a daughter in middle school, a job he is good at, a house with a garden he tends carefully on weekends. He had, by his own account, always been someone who believed that if you planned carefully enough, bad things could be managed or avoided altogether. That belief did not survive the flooding.

Three years ago, Omar and his family were visiting his in-laws in a small city in the south when a slow-moving storm system stalled overhead for four days. The rivers rose faster than anyone expected. He remembers standing at a window watching the street become a canal, telling his wife it would stop, it would stop, it would stop. It did not stop. The water came through the door. His mother-in-law, a woman in her seventies with a bad hip, could not move quickly. Omar carried her on his back through chest-high water to a neighbor's second floor while his daughter clung to his wife behind him. The current was stronger than he had imagined water could be. At one point he lost his footing and went under. He came back up. He does not talk easily about those seconds beneath the surface.

Everyone survived. He repeats this when he tells the story, as though he is trying to convince himself it is the most important fact. Everyone survived. And yet Omar has not returned to anything resembling the life he had before.

He sleeps badly. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with his heart hammering, the sheets damp, a sensation of cold water in his chest that he cannot explain to his wife in any way that feels adequate. He has stopped drinking coffee because the racing heart it produces frightens him. At work, he sits in front of two monitors writing code for a financial services company, and he is still competent - he is proud of that - but he has noticed that when it rains and the sound fills the open-plan office, he finds it nearly impossible to concentrate. He will read the same function three times and retain nothing. He has started wearing headphones even when he is not listening to anything.

He avoids the news when there are storms anywhere. He changed the route he drives to school pickup so he does not pass over the bridge above the creek near their neighborhood. He has not told his wife about the bridge. He has not told her about a great many things, because she was there too, and he believes - wrongly, probably, but with real conviction - that talking about it will make it worse for her.

What troubles him most, he says, is that he no longer trusts his own judgment. He was the one who said it would stop. He was the one who believed the plan would hold. He describes a persistent, low-grade vigilance that never fully lifts - checking weather applications multiple times a day, scanning the sky when he takes out the trash, feeling a tightening in his chest whenever his daughter mentions a school trip that involves water. He describes himself as a man who used to solve problems and now mostly manages fear.

He came to therapy, he says, because his daughter asked him why he never swims with her anymore. She is twelve and she asked the question simply, the way children do. He went to his car afterward and sat in the parking lot for twenty minutes before he could drive. He does not want to be the kind of father whose damage becomes something his daughter has to work around. That, more than anything else, is what brought him through the door.

output.reasoning: Quote: 'At one point he lost his footing and went under.' This sentence explicitly describes a direct experience of a life-threatening event (near-drowning during a flood), which meets DSM-5 Criterion A for a traumatic event involving threat of death or serious injury.
output.rationale: The vignette clearly describes a direct threat of death from drowning during a flood, satisfying Criterion A.
